solution:
Diethylamine is a secondary amine, so its single nitrogen-bonded hydrogen is replaced by the arenesulfonyl group (section 13.8):

\(\mathrm{p\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-SO_2Cl} + \mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{p\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-SO_2-N(C_2H_5)_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product is N,N-diethyl-p-toluenesulfonamide. It carries no hydrogen on nitrogen, so by the chapter's own reasoning it is not acidic and does not dissolve in alkali. [Note: this chapter discusses only benzenesulfonyl chloride \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) (Hinsberg's reagent) and never names p-toluenesulfonyl chloride; the reaction above is that same reaction applied to the p-methyl analogue, which differs only in the methyl group on the ring.]

Two moles of methyl bromide are required.

Ethanamine \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2}\) is a primary amine and N,N-dimethylethanamine \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-N(CH_3)_2}\) is a tertiary amine, so two of the nitrogen's hydrogen atoms have to be replaced by methyl groups. Section 13.6.2 gives the stepwise alkylation \(\mathrm{R-NH_2} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{HX}]{\mathrm{R\text{-}X}} \mathrm{R_2NH} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{HX}]{\mathrm{R\text{-}X}} \mathrm{R_3N}\), one mole of alkyl halide consumed at each step:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{CH_3Br} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-CH_3} + \mathrm{HBr}\)

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3Br} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5-N(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{HBr}\)

This agrees with the chapter's statement that a primary amine consumes three moles of alkyl halide to reach the quaternary ammonium salt: stopping one step earlier, at the tertiary amine, consumes two.

Propanamide (propionamide), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-NH_2}\).

Section 13.3.6 states that Hofmann degradation converts an amide into a primary amine containing ONE CARBON LESS. Ethanamine has two carbon atoms, so the amide must have three:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

This is the chapter's own general equation with \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-}\); note that ethanamide (acetamide) would give methylamine, not ethanamine.

In the gaseous phase the order of basicity is

\(\mathrm{R_3N} > \mathrm{R_2NH} > \mathrm{R-NH_2} > \mathrm{NH_3}\)

that is, tertiary > secondary > primary > ammonia.

Section 13.5.1 identifies TWO factors that stabilise the conjugate acid of an amine: the electron-releasing \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect of the alkyl groups, which increases with their number, and solvation by water, which decreases with their number because the number of hydrogen atoms on \(\mathrm{N^{\oplus}}\) available for hydrogen bonding falls from four in \(\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}}\) to one in \(\mathrm{R_3NH^{\oplus}}\). The chapter states that these two influences 'operate in opposite directions', and that it is the poor solvation of \(\mathrm{R_3NH^{\oplus}}\) that makes a tertiary amine a weaker base than a secondary one in aqueous medium. In the gaseous phase there is no solvent, so the solvation factor is absent and only the \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect operates. What is then observed is exactly the chapter's printed 'Expected order of basic strength', \(\mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{R-NH_2} < \mathrm{R_2NH} < \mathrm{R_3N}\). [Note: the phrase 'gaseous phase' does not occur anywhere in this chapter; the order above is the chapter's own \(+\mathrm{I}\)-only expected order, read with the solvation term removed.]

Because the alkyl group stabilises the conjugate acid, which shifts the basic equilibrium to the right.

Section 13.5 writes the equilibrium \(\mathrm{{\gg}N{:}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{{\gg}N^{\oplus}\text{-}H} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) and states that the more stabilised the conjugate acid, the further right this equilibrium lies and the stronger the base. Section 13.5.1(a) then explains that an alkyl group 'exerts electron releasing inductive effect \((+\mathrm{I})\) which stabilizes positive charge on atom bonded to it'. The conjugate acid of a primary aliphatic amine, \(\mathrm{R-NH_3^{\oplus}}\), carries one such alkyl group whereas the conjugate acid of ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}}\), carries none, so \(\mathrm{R-NH_3^{\oplus}}\) is the better stabilised of the two and the amine is the stronger base. Table 13.4 bears this out: methanamine has \(\mathrm{pK_b} = 3.38\) against \(4.75\) for ammonia, and a smaller \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a stronger base.

The product is aniline (benzenamine).

Section 13.3.2 states that aliphatic and aromatic nitrocompounds are reduced to primary amines by a metal-acid mixture such as Sn/HCl, and gives \(\mathrm{R-NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn/HCl}} \mathrm{R-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\). With nitrobenzene:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn/conc.\ HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Phenylmethanamine.

Benzylamine is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-NH_2}\), and Table 13.2 lists it under primary amines with the common name Benzylamine and the IUPAC name Phenylmethanamine. The name follows the rule of section 13.2.2: the carbon skeleton carrying the amino group is a one-carbon (methane) unit bearing a phenyl substituent, so the parent is methanamine and the substituent prefix is phenyl.

Increasing order of boiling points:

trimethylamine < ethylmethylamine < n-propylamine

All three are isomers of \(\mathrm{C_3H_9N}\), so molar mass is not the discriminator. Section 13.4.1 states the order for isomeric amines directly - 'primary amine > secondary amine > tertiary amine' - and explains it by intermolecular hydrogen bonding: n-propylamine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\) is primary and has two hydrogen atoms on nitrogen, ethylmethylamine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH-CH_3}\) is secondary and has one, and trimethylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) is tertiary and has none, so it can only manage the weaker dipole-dipole attraction. Table 13.3 shows the same pattern for the corresponding \(\mathrm{C_4}\) set: 350.8 K, 329.3 K and 310.5 K for serial numbers 1, 2 and 3.

Diethylamine is a base, so with dilute sulfuric acid it forms a substituted ammonium salt. Section 13.6.1(a) gives the general step \(\mathrm{{\gg}N{:}} + \mathrm{HCl(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{{\gg}N^{\oplus}\text{-}H(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}(aq)}\); sulfuric acid is dibasic, so two salts are possible depending on the proportions:

\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH_2^{\oplus}\ HSO_4^{\ominus}}\)  (diethylammonium hydrogensulfate)

\(2\,\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[(C_2H_5)_2NH_2^{\oplus}]_2\ SO_4^{2-}}\)  (diethylammonium sulfate)

The chapter itself shows the 1:1 pattern for an aromatic amine in section 13.9(c), where aniline and sulfuric acid give anilinium hydrogensulfate.

Increasing order of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\):

Cyclohexylamine < Aniline < 4-Nitroaniline

A larger \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a weaker base (section 13.5), so this is the order of decreasing basic strength. Cyclohexylamine (Table 13.2) is a primary ALIPHATIC amine, and section 13.5.2 states that 'arylamines in general are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines', so it has the smallest \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) of the three; Table 13.4 puts the primary alkanamines near 3.3-3.4 against 9.38 for aniline. In aniline the nitrogen lone pair 'is conjugated to the aromatic ring and is less available for protonation', which is why its \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) is so much larger. In 4-nitroaniline the nitro group at the para position draws electron density out of the ring, pulling the lone pair away from nitrogen still further, so the lone pair is even less available and the base is weaker again. [Note: this chapter tabulates no \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) for cyclohexylamine or for 4-nitroaniline, and it never uses the term 'electron-withdrawing' - its own 'Internet my friend' box asks the student to look up the nitroaniline values elsewhere. The placement of 4-nitroaniline above aniline therefore rests on extending the chapter's own lone-pair-availability argument, not on a printed value.]
